Though it occurs just once in the New Testament, the adjective form was common in everyday Koine, showing up in papyri where people sought to be secured "without trouble" from liabilities or debts (e.g., a tax document from 157 B.C.). The note in the Majority Standard Bible labeling this "promote" likely reflects how the surrounding phrase was rendered rather than the word itself, which all sources agree means "without distraction."
prose.caution: This word appears only once in the New Testament, and the measured rendering "promote" seems to capture the phrase rather than the word's actual meaning of "without distraction."

prose.def: Literally uncircumcised; used figuratively for people who are stubborn and resistant to God.
prose.article: The word literally means "uncircumcised," and in its single New Testament appearance (Acts 7:51) it is used figuratively—Stephen calls his hearers stubborn and resistant in heart and ears, which the Majority Standard Bible renders "stiff." In the Septuagint it occurs 34 times across 12 books, almost always translating the Hebrew עָרֵל ("uncircumcised," 30×), and it sometimes pairs metaphorically with "heart," as in Jeremiah 9:26. Interestingly, scholars suggest this blunt word may have been coined by Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria to express their contempt for the uncircumcised, since Egyptians normally used a milder term.

prose.def: To go away, depart, or leave from one place toward another.
prose.article: This common verb, built from "from" (ἀπό) plus "come/go" (ἔρχομαι), simply means to leave a place and head somewhere else; over half its 119 New Testament uses are rendered "went" and another fifth "went away." It often comes with a destination or direction, and in a special construction (with ὀπίσω) it means to "go after" or follow someone. In the Septuagint it appears 191 times, usually translating the Hebrew verb meaning "to walk" or "go" (114× for יָלַך), and the papyri show a touching everyday sense where a Christian epitaph uses it for someone who "departed" into a bright land.

The notable point is that this impersonal sense "it is enough" appears in Mark 14:41, where the underlying idea of "having in full" shades into "that's sufficient."

prose.def: To hold something back or keep away from it; or, when receiving payment, to have something in full.
prose.article: ἀπέχω covers a surprisingly wide range. Most often in the New Testament it means to keep oneself away from something — to abstain (rendered "abstain" in 56% of cases, e.g. Acts 15:20, 1 Thessalonians 4:3, 1 Peter 2:11) — but it can also mean to be physically distant from a place. Its most striking sense comes from everyday Koine receipts: the papyri and ostraca repeatedly use ἀπέχω to mean "I have received in full," which sharpens Jesus' warning that hypocrites "already have their reward in full" — they can sign the receipt, and nothing more is coming (Matthew 6:2, 6:5, 6:16). In the Septuagint it appears 9 times, most often translating the Hebrew רָחַק ("to be far").
prose.caution: The senses range from "abstain" to "receive in full" to "be distant," so context determines meaning, and translators differ noticeably on the Matthew 6 "reward in full" passages.

prose.def: To not believe something, refuse to trust, or fail to remain faithful.
prose.article: ἀπιστέω covers two related ideas: refusing to believe a report and failing to stay faithful. In the Byzantine New Testament it appears 7 times, and about half the renderings (3×) are simply "believe" (in the negative), as when the disciples did not believe the report of the risen Jesus (Mark 16:11, Luke 24:11). Everyday Koine papyri use it the same way — one Oxyrhynchus letter from the 2nd century AD promises to add "a fact which will excite your wonder and disbelief" until the documents are read. In a few places, notably Romans 3:3 and 2 Timothy 2:13, it shades toward unfaithfulness rather than mere disbelief, and Abbott-Smith notes some scholars even tie it to "disobey."

CONTEXTUAL FIT: The definition frames the word as active-voice transitive ('to store something up') but the Moulton-Milligan citations include a middle/participial form (ἀποθησαυριζομένων, genitive plural middle/passive participle), suggesting the word can also operate in middle voice; the definition does not acknowledge this morphological range.

SUPPORTING ARTICLE: The article says the word appears 'just once' in the NT and flags thin evidence as a caution, which is accurate, but the caution is presented as an 'interesting' footnote rather than integrated into the definition itself — readers deserve that qualification upfront.

SENSE LABELS: The single sense label 'storing up as treasure' is adequate but the definition does not capture the forward-looking, eschatological nuance present in 1TI 6:19, where storing up functions as laying hold of life to come — a theologically significant dimension the plain definition omits.

receipts.how: The only NT occurrence, where wealthy believers are urged to be rich in good deeds, ἀποθησαυρίζοντας — laying up/treasuring up as a foundation for the coming age, confirming the core sense but also its participial form and eschatological direction.

The forward-looking phrase 'foundation for the coming age' in context shows the definition's neutral 'for future use' partially fits but undersells the eschatological register that is central to the word's only NT use.

why: ἀποθλίβω occurs only once in the Byzantine New Testament (Luke 8:45), so its range of meaning cannot be established from New Testament usage alone — treat any single gloss cautiously.
There the Majority Standard Bible renders it “against”.
In the Septuagint it appears 1 time, most often translating the Hebrew לָחַץ (H3905) (1×).

prose.def: To press hard against someone from every side, as in a crowd squeezing in on a person.
prose.article: ἀποθλίβω describes the action of a crowd squeezing in hard on someone from all sides. It appears just once in the Byzantine New Testament, at Luke 8:45, where the crowds 'press against' Jesus, and once in the Septuagint, where it renders the Hebrew לָחַץ in Numbers 22:25 — the scene of Balaam's donkey crushing his foot against a wall. Moulton-Milligan find the word in everyday Koine papyri, including a 116 BC document about people being 'pressed' or hard-pressed, confirming its use beyond the Bible.
prose.caution: With only one New Testament occurrence and one Septuagint use, the evidence for its full range is thin.

Dodson lists a literal gloss 'I rub' and the nuance 'jostle,' which the current definition omits — the definition's 'press hard from every side' is reasonable but does not capture the rubbing/jostling component attested in the classical sources.

The Moulton-Milligan papyrus use suggests a metaphorical or legal sense of being 'hard-pressed' (pressed into a corner, having no legal recourse), which the current definition entirely ignores by limiting the word to a physical crowd scene.
The single sense label '1. pressing or crowding against' is serviceable but too narrow given the lexical evidence from Dodson and MM showing broader application.

receipts.how: The only NT occurrence, where the crowd presses against Jesus, directly supports the core physical-crowding sense the definition describes.

The MM papyrus (P Tor I, 116 BC) shows the word used in a non-crowd, non-physical context of people being hard-pressed legally, demonstrating the definition is too narrow in restricting the word to physical crowding from every side.
Dodson's gloss 'jostle' alongside 'press hard' suggests lateral or incidental contact rather than uniform all-sided squeezing, a nuance the current definition overstates with 'from every side.'

The Majority Standard Bible — translated from this same Greek text — renders it “died” in 80 of those places (85%), e.g. Matthew 8:32; Mark 12:20. This is observed translation data, not an editorial opinion.
The Berean Standard Bible, an independent translation, agrees with that rendering in 99% of the same verses.
The sense “died” is independently listed by Dodson, Strong's, the KJV glosses, corroborating the corpus evidence.
Attested secondary renderings: “dies” (9×) — these mark the edges of its range, each verifiable at the citations given.
In the Septuagint it appears 485 times, most often translating the Hebrew מוּת (H4191) (403×).
Moulton–Milligan documents this word in everyday papyri and inscriptions, anchoring the meaning in ordinary Koine usage outside the New Testament.
High confidence: large sample, a dominant sense, independent translation agreement, and lexicon corroboration all converge.

prose.def: To die, whether by natural causes, violence, or in a spiritual sense of being dead to something.
prose.article: ἀποθνήσκω is the ordinary Koine verb for dying, and the Byzantine New Testament uses it 111 times across 15 books, almost always rendered "died" (80×, 85%) or "dies" (9×, 10%). Its range covers natural death, violent death (as the passive counterpart of "kill"), and a figurative spiritual death, as in being dead to sin or to the law. In the Septuagint it appears a striking 485 times, mostly translating the Hebrew verb מוּת ("to die") 403 times, showing how thoroughly it served as the standard word for death.

issues: The syntactic role data shows 'vocative (109×)' which is almost certainly a data artifact or mislabeling, yet the definition makes no attempt to clarify the verb's actual syntactic behavior (active, middle, passive roles) across its 111 occurrences

The sense labels '1. died; 2. dies' cover only tense/aspect variation (past vs. present) and do not reflect the semantically distinct sub-senses identified in Abbott-Smith and the classical lexica: natural death, violent death (passive counterpart of ἀποκτείνω), spiritual death, and the dative-of-reference construction (dying to something)

'Being dead to something' (dative of reference, e.g. ROM 6:2, GAL 2:19) is a grammatically and theologically distinct construction that the definition conflates under 'spiritual sense of being dead to something' without making clear it is a dative construction, not a different meaning of the verb itself
The 17× absorbed into phrasing (15% of occurrences) are unaccounted for in the sense labels and the article, representing a non-trivial gap
Dodson's gloss 'am about to die, wither, decay' introduces an ingressive or progressive nuance not mentioned in the definition

receipts.how: Demonstrates the dative-of-reference construction ('died to sin') where the verb does not simply mean 'died' but encodes a relational severance, showing the current sense labels are too narrow.
Illustrates spiritual death ('so that one may eat of it and not die'), confirming the figurative sense the definition acknowledges but the sense labels entirely omit.
Straightforward violent death of the swine, corroborating the primary 'died' sense and the preposition ἐν construction noted in Abbott-Smith.

audit.author_note: Paul uses ἀποθνήσκω with striking theological density, especially the dative-of-reference construction (ROM 6:2, 6:10, GAL 2:19, COL 2:20) and the 'dying for/on behalf of' formula (ROM 5:6–8), while John uses it heavily for physical death with eschatological overtones (JOH 6:50, 8:21, 11:50–51); a definition calibrated to Paul's figurative usage will partially mislead readers of John.

prose.def: To bring something or someone back to a former, proper, or healthy condition; to restore or give back.
prose.article: ἀποκαθίστημι means to put something back the way it was—whether healing a body, returning a thing, or reestablishing affairs. In the Byzantine New Testament's 8 occurrences, the Majority Standard Bible renders it "restored" 7 times (88%), most often of physical healing like the withered hand in Matthew 12:13 and Mark 3:5. The everyday Koine papyri sharpen the "give back" side of the word: one early document uses it for making restitution, demanding that a defaulting priest's guarantors pay back what is owed.

issues: The syntactic role data reports 'vocative (8×)' which is almost certainly a data artifact, but the definition does not account for any non-restoration sense; Heb 13:19 uses the word in the sense of 'give back / bring back' (returning a person), which is distinct from restoring something to a former condition and deserves explicit mention
The single sense label '1. restored to a former condition' does not capture the 'give back / bring back' usage attested in Heb 13:19, which Abbott-Smith and Dodson both list as a separate sense
The definition phrase 'or give back' is present but is buried and not reflected in the sense label, leaving the Heb 13:19 usage under-represented
The supporting article focuses almost exclusively on physical healing; the eschatological/political restoration sense (MAT 17:11, MAR 9:12, ACT 1:6) is not mentioned in the definition or labels

receipts.how: The hand is 'restored' to health, directly confirming the primary sense of returning something to a former, healthy condition.
The disciples ask whether Jesus will 'restore' the kingdom to Israel, demonstrating the political/eschatological restoration sense that the definition's article does not address.
Paul urges prayer so he may be 'restored' (brought back) to them, representing the 'give back / bring back a person' sense that the single sense label omits.

audit.author_note: Luke-Acts uses the word both for physical healing (LUK 6:10) and for eschatological-political restoration (ACT 1:6), while Hebrews uses it in the personal sense of returning someone to a community (HEB 13:19); readers of different books encounter meaningfully different nuances.
